pos: adv. and a. (toward the east; in Scripture the direction of Eden, of the tabernacle door, and of the returning glory)
etymology: From east (Anglo-Saxon east, the quarter of the dawn) plus the directional suffix -ward, meaning turned toward. The Hebrew for east, qedem, also means front and ancient — the Hebrew orients himself facing the sunrise, so that east is before him and the past is before him too.
biblical_def: Eastward is the most theologically freighted compass point in Scripture. The garden is planted there: “the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed” (Gen 2:8) — and when the man is driven out, cherubim are set at the east of the garden to keep the way of the tree of life, so that the road back to God lies east and is barred. The tabernacle repeats the geography deliberately: the only door faces east, and immediately before it “shall be Moses, and Aaron and his sons, keeping the charge of the sanctuary” (Num 3:38) — the priesthood camped exactly where the cherubim stood, guarding the same approach. And Ezekiel sees the return: “the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east” (Eze 43:4) — the glory that had departed eastward comes back by the same road. To Abram, standing between promise and possession, the LORD says, “Lift up now thine eyes… northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward” (Gen 13:14), and the whole land is given by looking.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eastward as toward the east, in the direction of the rising sun — and notes the east as the quarter of the sunrise, whence the ancient orientation of temples and of maps.
webster_full: EASTWARD, adv. Toward the east; in the direction of east; as, to move eastward.
EAST, n. The point in the heavens where the sun is seen to rise at the equinox, or the corresponding point on the earth.
2. In Scripture, the east is often put for the front, as the Hebrews reckoned the quarters facing the rising sun.
Note. Hence in Hebrew the same word denotes the east and that which is before or ancient.
scriptures: Gen 2:8
And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.
Num 3:38

But those that encamp before the tabernacle toward the east, even before the tabernacle of the congregation eastward, shall be Moses, and Aaron and his sons, keeping the charge of the sanctuary for the charge of the children of Israel; and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death.
Eze 43:4
And the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east.
And the LORD said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him, Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward:
corruption_summary: The sacred orientation of Scripture is either dismissed as borrowed Ancient Near Eastern architecture or seized upon by mystics as a spiritual technique.
corruption_paragraphs: The historical-critical habit is to note that other ancient temples also faced east and conclude that Israel simply absorbed regional convention. The direction of the argument is wrong. Scripture gives its own reason for the eastward door, and it is a narrative reason: the way back into the presence of God was closed at the east of Eden, and every subsequent sanctuary reopens that same approach under guard, under blood, and by appointment. The tabernacle is not borrowed architecture; it is a theological argument in fabric and gold, and Moses is told to make it after the pattern shewed him in the mount (Exo 25:40).

The opposite error treats compass directions as channels of spiritual power — praying eastward for enlightenment, arranging a room for spiritual flow. That is not devotion but divination, and the same Ezekiel who saw the glory return by the east gate had earlier seen men in the temple “with their faces toward the east; and they worshipped the sun toward the east” (Eze 8:16), which is named as an abomination. The eastward door means what God says it means: there is one way in, He appointed it, and He has posted a guard at it.
roots_summary: English east + -ward; rendering Hebrew qedem (H6924), east, front, aforetime, and mizrach (H4217), the place of the sun's rising.
roots_lines: Hebrew qedem (H6924) — east, front, ancient time; the Hebrew faces the sunrise, so before him is both east and the past.
Hebrew miqqedem — “eastward” in Gen 2:8, and “at the east” of the garden where the cherubim are placed (Gen 3:24).
Hebrew mizrach (H4217) — the rising, the east quarter; from zarach, to rise, said of the sun.
Anglo-Saxon -weard — turned toward; the suffix of eastward, homeward, toward.
Mat 2:1 — the wise men come “from the east”, and Mat 24:27 makes the lightning that cometh out of the east the figure of Christ's coming.
usage: “A garden eastward in Eden” — and the way back barred at the east by cherubim.
“Before the tabernacle… eastward” — the priests camped where the cherubim stood.
“By the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east” — the glory returning by the road it left.

pos: adv. and a. (toward the west; in the tabernacle, the closed end — the side where the holy of holies stood and no door was)
etymology: From west (Anglo-Saxon west, the quarter of the sunset) plus -ward. Hebrew has no separate word for the west: it says yam, the sea, because the Mediterranean lay westward of the land, and it says achor, behind, because a man facing east has the west at his back.
biblical_def: Westward in the Law is nearly always structural, and its structure preaches. The tabernacle's west end is closed: “for the sides of the tabernacle westward thou shalt make six boards” (Exo 26:22) — boards, not a curtain and not a door. The most holy place stood at that end, and there was no way in from behind. Only one man, once a year, with blood, entered from the east through the veil. Behind that closed wall camped the Gershonites: “The families of the Gershonites shall pitch behind the tabernacle westward” (Num 3:23). The word also marks the boundary of sight and of longing. Abram is told to look “northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward” (Gen 13:14) and given all he sees; Moses on Pisgah is told to lift his eyes “westward, and northward, and southward, and eastward, and behold it with thine eyes: for thou shalt not go over this Jordan” (Deu 3:27) — the same four directions, the same gift of sight, and a man who will see the land and not enter it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines westward as toward the west, and the west as the quarter where the sun sets, the point directly opposite to the east.
webster_full: WESTWARD, adv. Toward the west; as, to sail westward.
WEST, n. That point of the horizon where the sun sets at the equinox; or the corresponding point of the earth.
2. A region or country lying in that direction.
Note. In the Hebrew the west is denoted by the sea, the Mediterranean lying west of Judea, and also by the word signifying behind.
scriptures: And for the sides of the tabernacle westward thou shalt make six boards.
Num 3:23
The families of the Gershonites shall pitch behind the tabernacle westward.
Deu 3:27
Get thee up into the top of Pisgah, and lift up thine eyes westward, and northward, and southward, and eastward, and behold it with thine eyes: for thou shalt not go over this Jordan.
And the LORD said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him, Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that God appointed one way into His presence and closed every other.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No movement disputes which way is west. What has been lost is the doctrine the tabernacle's closed west end was built to teach: that access to God is not available on every side, that the sinner does not select his own approach, and that the one way in is the way God appointed. Exo 26:22 specifies boards where a man might have expected an opening, and the specification is deliberate. Behind the mercy seat there was a wall.

The principle to recover is exclusivity of access, which the New Testament does not abolish but fulfils. “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6); “having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way” (Heb 10:19-20). The veil is torn and the way is open — but it is still a way, singular, and it is still the one God opened. Deu 3:27 supplies the sober companion truth: Moses saw the whole land from Pisgah, in every direction, and did not enter. Sight is not possession, and no amount of looking substitutes for the appointed entrance.
roots_summary: English west + -ward; rendering Hebrew yam (H3220), the sea, used for the west quarter, and achor (H268), the hinder part.
roots_lines: Hebrew yam (H3220) — sea; used for “west” because the Great Sea lay west of the land. “Westward” in Exo 26:22 is literally “seaward”.
Hebrew achor (H268) — the hinder part, behind; the west is behind a man facing the sunrise.
Hebrew maarab (H4628) — the setting, the west; from arab, to grow dark, whence also evening.
Psa 103:12 — “as far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us”; the one pair of directions with no meeting point.
Num 3:23-38 — the four Levite camps by compass: Gershon west, Kohath south, Merari north, Moses and Aaron east at the door.
usage: “For the sides of the tabernacle westward… six boards” — a wall where a man might expect a door.
“Pitch behind the tabernacle westward” — the Gershonites at the closed end.
“Lift up thine eyes westward… for thou shalt not go over” — sight granted, entrance withheld.

pos: adv. and a. (toward the north; in Scripture the quarter of the Levites of Merari, and of the invader's road)
etymology: From north (Anglo-Saxon north) plus -ward. Hebrew tsaphon means the north and also the hidden or dark quarter — the side of the sky the sun never crosses in the northern hemisphere.
biblical_def: Northward orders the camp and, in the prophets, announces the invader. In the wilderness the compass assigns duty: “these shall pitch on the side of the tabernacle northward” (Num 3:35) — the sons of Merari, who carried the boards, bars, pillars and sockets, the heavy frame of the whole structure. But the north is also the road every conqueror took into the land, because the desert forbade a direct approach from the east; Assyria and Babylon both came down from the north, and Jeremiah's call begins with a seething pot “toward the north” and the verdict “Out of the north an evil shall break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land” (Jer 1:14). Deuteronomy gives the word its most bracing use. Israel has been circling: “Ye have compassed this mountain long enough: turn you northward” (Deu 2:3). After thirty-eight years of going round the same hill, the command is simply to change direction and go on — which is the plainest picture of repentance in the Pentateuch.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines northward as toward the north, and the north as the point of the horizon directly opposite the sun at midday in the northern latitudes.
webster_full: NORTHWARD, adv. Toward the north, or toward a point nearer to the north than the east and west points.
NORTH, n. One of the cardinal points, being that point of the horizon which is directly opposite to the sun in the meridian.
2. Any region or country situated north of another.
Note. Out of the north an evil shall break forth. Jer. i.
scriptures: Deu 2:3
Ye have compassed this mountain long enough: turn you northward.
Num 3:35
And the chief of the house of the father of the families of Merari was Zuriel the son of Abihail: these shall pitch on the side of the tabernacle northward.
Deu 3:27
Get thee up into the top of Pisgah, and lift up thine eyes westward, and northward, and southward, and eastward, and behold it with thine eyes: for thou shalt not go over this Jordan.
And the LORD said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him, Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward:
corruption_summary: Deu 2:3 is domesticated into a slogan about personal breakthrough, when the command comes to a nation under judgment and means a change of direction, not a change of feeling.
corruption_paragraphs: “Ye have compassed this mountain long enough” has become a favourite of motivational preaching, where it is applied to career stagnation and unrealised dreams. The context is a generation dying in the wilderness under a sworn judgment for unbelief at Kadesh. The circling was not bad luck; it was a sentence. And what ends it is not a burst of confidence but a plain command to turn and go a different way — which is what repentance is. Reduce the verse to a promise of momentum and you have kept the encouragement and discarded the judgment that made it necessary.

The prophetic north supplies the other half. When Jeremiah is shown the seething pot facing north, he is being told that the invader is God's appointed rod, not a geopolitical accident — the same doctrine Isaiah states when he calls Assyria “the rod of mine anger” (Isa 10:5). Modern readings that treat the exile as ordinary Ancient Near Eastern power politics with a theological gloss added afterward invert the prophets' own claim. The armies came from the north because God summoned them, and they went home again when He was done.
roots_summary: English north + -ward; rendering Hebrew tsaphon (H6828), the north, the hidden quarter, from tsaphan, to hide or store up.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaphon (H6828) — north; from tsaphan, to hide, the dark quarter the sun does not cross.
Hebrew tsaphonah — northward, with the directional ending -ah; the form in Deu 2:3 and Num 3:35.
Jer 1:13-14 — the seething pot “toward the north”, and the evil that breaks forth from thence; the road of Assyria and Babylon.
Psa 75:6 — “promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south”; the north is pointedly omitted, whence God Himself.
Isa 14:13 — “I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north”; the boast of the king of Babylon.
usage: “Turn you northward” — the end of thirty-eight years of circling one hill.
“Pitch on the side of the tabernacle northward” — Merari, who bore the frame.
“Out of the north an evil shall break forth” — the invader's road, and God's summons.

pos: adv. and a. (toward the south; the tabernacle's lamp side, and the quarter of the Negev and of drought)
etymology: From south (Anglo-Saxon suth) plus -ward. Hebrew uses negev, the parched land, for the south, and teman, the right hand — because a man facing the sunrise has the south on his right.
biblical_def: Southward in the Law is the lamp side. When the tabernacle is set up, “he put the candlestick in the tent of the congregation, over against the table, on the side of the tabernacle southward” (Exo 40:24) — the golden lampstand on the south, the table of shewbread on the north, the two facing each other across the holy place, light and bread together, as they are together in the Lord's own self-descriptions. The framing matches: “twenty boards on the south side southward” (Exo 26:18). And the camp matches: “The families of the sons of Kohath shall pitch on the side of the tabernacle southward” (Num 3:29) — Kohath, who carried the ark, the table, the candlestick and the altars, the holy furniture itself, on staves and on shoulders. Outside the sanctuary, the south is the Negev, the dry country of Abraham's sojourning and Isaac's wells, and Psalm 126 prays for its wadis to run again: “Turn again our captivity, O LORD, as the streams in the south.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines southward as toward the south, and the south as the point of the horizon directly opposite the north, on the right hand of one facing the east.
webster_full: SOUTHWARD, adv. Toward the south; as, to sail southward.
SOUTH, n. The meridian point which the sun crosses at noon in northern latitudes; one of the cardinal points.
2. A southern region or country.
Note. In the Hebrew the south is called the right hand, as the quarters were reckoned by one facing the east.
Note. The south is also called the Negeb, or dry land, from its parched character.
scriptures: And he put the candlestick in the tent of the congregation, over against the table, on the side of the tabernacle southward.
And thou shalt make the boards for the tabernacle, twenty boards on the south side southward.
Num 3:29
The families of the sons of Kohath shall pitch on the side of the tabernacle southward.
Deu 3:27
Get thee up into the top of Pisgah, and lift up thine eyes westward, and northward, and southward, and eastward, and behold it with thine eyes: for thou shalt not go over this Jordan.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; what is neglected is the tabernacle's deliberate arrangement, which modern readers skim as inventory rather than read as doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The chapters that specify boards on the south side and Levite families camped by compass point are among the most skipped in Scripture, treated as an ancient building schedule of no present use. But the precision is the point: God specified where the light stood and where the bread stood and who camped where and who carried what, and He specified it because the whole structure was a shadow of good things to come (Heb 10:1). Skimming the measurements is skimming the sermon.

The principle to recover is that God is a God of order, and that His order extends to arrangements men would call incidental. The lampstand faced the table; the priests carried the holy things on their shoulders and never on a cart, a lesson Uzzah's death later enforced (2Sa 6:6-7); each family had its side and its burden. Where that instinct is lost, worship drifts toward whatever seems effective, and the regulative principle — that God appoints the manner of His own worship and not merely the fact of it — is quietly abandoned.
roots_summary: English south + -ward; rendering Hebrew negev (H5045), the parched south country, teman (H8486), the right hand or south, and darom (H1864), the south.
roots_lines: Hebrew negev (H5045) — the dry, parched land; hence the south country, and the proper name Negeb.
Hebrew teman (H8486) — the right hand, hence the south; the Hebrew orients facing east.
Hebrew darom (H1864) — the south; used chiefly in Ezekiel's temple vision.
Hebrew negbah — southward, with the directional ending; the form of Exo 26:18 and Num 3:29.
Psa 126:4 — “as the streams in the south”, the sudden filling of dry wadis, a figure for a restored captivity.
usage: “The candlestick… on the side of the tabernacle southward” — the lamp facing the bread.
“Twenty boards on the south side southward” — a measured house, not an improvised one.
“Kohath shall pitch… southward” — nearest the holy things they were to bear.

pos: adv. and a. (toward a higher place; in Scripture the direction of fruit, of trouble, and of the eyes lifted in prayer)
etymology: From up (Anglo-Saxon up) plus -ward, turned toward. It is one of the oldest English compounds and has not changed its sense in a thousand years.
biblical_def: Upward occurs at three memorable places. It is the direction of fruit in the promise to Hezekiah's besieged remnant: “the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall yet again take root downward, and bear fruit upward” (2Ki 19:30; repeated at Isa 37:31). Roots first, and hidden, and downward; fruit afterward, and visible, and upward — the order is fixed, and it is the order of the Christian life, in which what is seen grows out of what is not. It is the direction of trouble in Eliphaz's proverb: “man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward” (Job 5:7) — a saying true in itself, though the comforter misapplies it to Job. Trouble rises out of fallen human life as naturally and as inevitably as sparks rise out of a fire; it needs no explanation beyond the fall. And it is the measure of the flood's completeness: “Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail” (Gen 7:20). The lifting of eyes and hands upward is the posture of prayer throughout Scripture.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines upward as toward a higher place, and also as more, or above a stated quantity, as in a hundred and upward.
webster_full: UPWARD, adv. In a direction from lower to higher; toward a higher place.
Looking upward to heaven.
2. Toward the source or origin; as, to trace a family upward.
3. More; indefinitely more; above; as a hundred and upward.
Note. From twenty years old and upward. Num. i.
scriptures: And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall yet again take root downward, and bear fruit upward.
And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward:
Job 5:7
Yet man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward.
Gen 7:20
Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail; and the mountains were covered.
corruption_summary: Job 5:7 is quoted as though the book endorsed Eliphaz, and the root-and-fruit promise is reversed into a demand for visible fruit before any hidden rooting has occurred.
corruption_paragraphs: Eliphaz says many true things and draws a false conclusion from them, and God's verdict at the end of the book is that Job's comforters “have not spoken of me the thing that is right” (Job 42:7). It is therefore careless to quote Job 5:7 as a simple statement of biblical doctrine without noting who says it and why: Eliphaz is arguing that trouble follows sin, and therefore Job's trouble proves Job's sin. The proverb is sound; the syllogism it serves is exactly what the book was written to demolish. Every quotation from the book of Job needs the speaker named.

The root-and-fruit order in 2Ki 19:30 rebukes a different impatience. Modern ministry frequently demands fruit upward — visible growth, measurable results, testimony — from converts and churches that have not yet rooted downward in the ordinary, unglamorous, invisible means: the word read and preached, prayer, the ordinances, the fellowship of the saints. God's promise to a remnant reduced to almost nothing is that He will do it in the right order and in His own time. A tree hurried into fruit before it has rooted is a tree that will not survive the first dry summer.
roots_summary: English up + -ward; rendering Hebrew maal (H4605), above, upward, and lemalah, to the upper part — also the idiom “and upward” in the census formulas.
roots_lines: Hebrew maal (H4605) — above, upward; from alah, to go up.
Hebrew lemalah — upward, to the top; “bear fruit upward” (2Ki 19:30) and “fifteen cubits upward” (Gen 7:20).
Hebrew wamaalah — “and upward”, the census formula “from twenty years old and upward” (Num 1:3).
Job 5:7 in Hebrew — bene resheph, “sons of the flame”, rendered sparks; they “lift up to fly”.
Joh 11:41 — “Jesus lifted up his eyes”; the ordinary posture of prayer in both Testaments is upward, not downward.
usage: “Take root downward, and bear fruit upward” — the hidden work first, always.
“As the sparks fly upward” — true in itself, and misapplied by the man who says it.
“From twenty years old and upward” — the census formula of Israel's muster.

pos: adv. and a. (toward the front; onward; in Scripture the command at the Red Sea and the direction Israel would not go)
etymology: From fore (Anglo-Saxon fore, before) plus -ward. The adjective sense of presumptuous is later and is not the Bible's.
biblical_def: Forward is the word of the one command God gives at the Red Sea. Israel is trapped, the sea before and Pharaoh behind, and Moses is praying: “And the LORD said unto Moses, Wherefore criest thou unto me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward” (Exo 14:15). The rebuke is startling — there is a time when further prayer is disobedience, because the command has already been given and only obedience remains. The word then governs the whole march: “When ye blow an alarm, then the camps that lie on the east parts shall go forward” (Num 10:5), the trumpet order by which the tribes moved in rank behind the cloud. Jeremiah uses it for the exact reverse, and it is his summary of the nation's history: “they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear, but walked in the counsels and in the imagination of their evil heart, and went backward, and not forward” (Jer 7:24). And Genesis uses it plainly of Isaac's increase: “the man waxed great, and went forward, and grew until he became very great” (Gen 26:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines forward as toward a part or place before or in front, onward, in progression — and, as an adjective, ready, prompt, or too ready and presumptuous.
webster_full: FORWARD, adv. Toward a part or place before or in front; onward; progressively.
Speak unto the children of Israel that they go forward. Ex. xiv.
FORWARD, a. Near or at the fore part; anterior.
2. Ready; prompt; strongly inclined; as, forward to serve.
3. Too ready; over-confident; presumptuous; bold.
scriptures: And the LORD said unto Moses, Wherefore criest thou unto me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward:
Num 10:5
When ye blow an alarm, then the camps that lie on the east parts shall go forward.
Jer 7:24
But they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear, but walked in the counsels and in the imagination of their evil heart, and went backward, and not forward.
And the man waxed great, and went forward, and grew until he became very great:
corruption_summary: Exo 14:15 is enlisted for a general gospel of forward motion — step out, take the leap — when the command is to a specific people, at a specific sea, on the strength of a specific promise.
corruption_paragraphs: “Go forward” is a favourite of the entrepreneurial-faith register, where it becomes divine authorisation for whatever venture the hearer already wanted to attempt. But Israel is not told to step out and see what happens; they are told to walk into a sea that God is about to divide, on the strength of an explicit word, having been told in the previous verse to stand still and see His salvation. Take away the promise and the command is not faith but presumption — which is precisely the sin the same generation commits at Kadesh when they go up without the ark and are beaten (Num 14:44-45).

The verse does carry a hard and legitimate rebuke. There is a moment when praying more is a way of not obeying, and Moses hits it: God has spoken, the path is named, and the crying becomes delay. The Puritan counsel is exact here — pray until you know the will of God, then act upon it, and do not use devotion as a place to hide. Jer 7:24 shows what the alternative looks like at national scale: not a dramatic apostasy but a slow going backward, one unheeded word at a time.
roots_summary: English fore + -ward; rendering Hebrew nasa (H5265), to pull up stakes and journey, and the idiom “go forward” for breaking camp.
roots_lines: Hebrew nasa (H5265) — to pull up tent pegs, to set out; the standard verb for Israel's marches, rendered “go forward” and “journey”.
Exo 14:15 — weyissau, “let them set out”; the command is to break camp and march into the sea.
Hebrew achor (H268) — backward; the opposite pole in Jer 7:24, “went backward, and not forward”.
Hebrew panim — face, front; the forward direction is the direction a man faces.
Php 3:13-14 — the New Testament's forward: forgetting what is behind, epekteinomenos, stretching out toward what is before.
usage: “That they go forward” — a command that made further prayer delay.
“The camps… shall go forward” — the trumpet order for breaking camp in rank.
“Went backward, and not forward” — a nation's history in five words.

pos: adv. (to or on one side; away from the direct course — in Scripture both the turning that sees God and the turning that leaves Him)
etymology: From a- (on) plus side. The prefix is the same locative a- as in afar, ashore, abroad: literally on the side.
biblical_def: Aside cuts both ways in Scripture, and the two directions are worth holding together. It can name the turning that sees God: “And Moses said, I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt” (Exo 3:3) — a shepherd interrupts his own errand to look at something strange, and God speaks out of the bush only after He sees that Moses turned aside. It can name the laying down of a hindrance: “let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us” (Heb 12:1) — where the weight need not be sinful to need laying aside; a runner sheds what is merely heavy as well as what is wrong. But it also names apostasy: “They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one” (Psa 14:3), which Paul quotes in Romans 3 as part of his indictment of the whole race. And it names the setting aside of Scripture: “laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men” (Mar 7:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines aside as on or to one side, out of a perpendicular or straight direction — and also as apart, in a state of separation, or out of the mind.
webster_full: ASIDE, adv. On or to one side; out of a perpendicular or straight direction.
2. At a little distance from the main part or body.
Thou shalt set aside that which is full. 2 Kings iv.
3. From the company; as, to take one aside.
4. Apart; out of the mind or thoughts; as, to lay aside all animosity.
scriptures: Exo 3:3
And Moses said, I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.
Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Psa 14:3
They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one.
Mar 7:8
For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do.
corruption_summary: Mar 7:8 is answered by every tradition-based system with the claim that it adds to Scripture rather than setting it aside — a distinction the Lord Himself refuses to grant.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord's charge against the Pharisees is not that they had extra customs but that the customs displaced the commandment: they had made the word of God of none effect through their tradition (Mar 7:13). Rome's answer, and the Eastern answer, is that tradition is a second stream of revelation which supplements without contradicting. But the moment a tradition binds the conscience with something Scripture has not commanded, the commandment has in fact been laid aside, because the sufficiency of Scripture is itself one of the things Scripture teaches. That is sola Scriptura in its actual sense: not that the church has no teachers, but that no teacher and no council may bind where God has not spoken.

Protestants are not exempt. Where a congregation's real authority is a denominational culture, a celebrated personality, or an unexamined set of expectations about what church must look like, the mechanism of Mar 7:8 is running whatever the doctrinal statement says. Heb 12:1 gives the discipline that answers it: lay aside every weight. Some of what a Christian carries is sin and must be repented of; some of it is merely accumulated, and must simply be put down.
roots_summary: English a- + side; rendering Hebrew sur (H5493), to turn aside, and Greek apotithemi (G659), to put off, and aphiemi (G863), to leave or let go.
roots_lines: Hebrew sur (H5493) — to turn aside, depart; Moses' “I will now turn aside” (Exo 3:3), and Exo 3:4, “when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see”.
Hebrew sug (H5472) — to backslide, turn away; “they are all gone aside” (Psa 14:3).
Greek apotithemi (G659) — to put off, as a garment; “lay aside every weight” (Heb 12:1), and “put off… the old man” (Eph 4:22).
Greek ogkos (G3591) — bulk, mass; the “weight” of Heb 12:1 is impedimenta, not necessarily sin.
Greek aphiemi (G863) — to leave, let go; “laying aside the commandment of God” (Mar 7:8).
usage: “I will now turn aside, and see” — and God spoke when He saw that he turned.
“Lay aside every weight” — a runner sheds what is heavy as well as what is wrong.
“Laying aside the commandment of God” — tradition that displaces rather than supplements.

pos: adv. and prep. (at the back of; remaining after; in Scripture the place of the disqualifying backward look and of the guiding voice)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon behindan — be- (by) plus hindan (from behind). The same hind survives in hindmost and hindrance.
biblical_def: Behind marks three things in Scripture. It is the place of the fatal backward look: “But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt” (Gen 19:26) — and the Lord Jesus makes it a standing warning: Remember Lot's wife (Luk 17:32). It is the place of what the Christian must deliberately forget: “forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before” (Php 3:13), where what Paul is putting behind him includes both his sins and his considerable religious credentials. But it is also, remarkably, the place of the guiding voice: “thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left” (Isa 30:21) — the shepherd walking behind the flock, correcting from the rear. And it is the position of humble faith: the woman with the issue of blood “came in the press behind, and touched his garment” (Mar 5:27), approaching from the back because she did not think herself fit to approach from the front, and going away healed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines behind as at the back of another, on the side opposite the front — and also as remaining after the departure of another, or left at a distance.
webster_full: BEHIND, prep. At the back of another; as, to ride behind a horseman.
2. On the back part, at any distance; in the rear; as, to walk behind another.
3. Remaining; left after the departure of another; as, he departed and left us behind.
4. Inferior to another in attainments; as, he is behind his companions in learning.
BEHIND, adv. Out of sight; not produced or exhibited to view; remaining.
scriptures: But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
Php 3:13
Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before,
And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.
Mar 5:27
When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment.
corruption_summary: Isa 30:21 is detached from its context and used as a promise of private mystical guidance, when the voice behind is the written word applied, and the chapter is a rebuke of Israel for seeking counsel elsewhere.
corruption_paragraphs: “This is the way, walk ye in it” is one of the most commonly claimed promises for decision-making, and it is usually claimed for an inner impression about a job, a move, or a marriage. The chapter is about a nation that went down to Egypt for help without asking at the mouth of the LORD, and that told the seers, “See not; and to the prophets, Prophesy not unto us right things” (Isa 30:10). The promised voice is the counsel they had refused — God's own instruction, restored to a chastened people. Its normal channel is the Scriptures, read and preached, applied by the Spirit to a conscience that wants to obey. That is a better guide than an impression, and it can be tested.

Gen 19:26 and Php 3:13 supply the discipline of the backward look. Lot's wife was not condemned for a glance but for a heart still in the city she had been carried out of; the look reported what the look revealed. Paul's forgetting is likewise not amnesia — he recites his own history freely, including his persecution of the church — but a refusal to live off it, whether the past is a source of shame or of pride. The credentials in Php 3 that he counts loss are impressive ones. What lies behind is not to be denied; it is not to be turned back toward.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon behindan; rendering Hebrew achar / achare (H310), after, behind, and Greek opiso (G3694), behind, backward, and opisthen (G3693), from behind.
roots_lines: Hebrew achar (H310) — after, behind; the same root as acharith, the latter end.
Hebrew meachar — “from behind”; Lot's wife looked back from behind him (Gen 19:26).
Greek opiso (G3694) — behind, back; “Get thee behind me, Satan” (Mat 16:23), and “come after me” in the call to discipleship.
Greek opisthen (G3693) — from behind; the woman who touched the hem (Mar 5:27; Luk 8:44).
Php 3:13 — epilanthanomenos, forgetting, a present participle: a continuing refusal to live off what is past.
usage: “Looked back from behind him” — a glance that reported where the heart still was.
“Forgetting those things which are behind” — including the credentials, not only the sins.
“A word behind thee” — the shepherd correcting from the rear.

pos: prep. and adv. (on the further side of; past a limit — in Scripture the limit a prophet may not cross and the distance the word need not be fetched from)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon begeondan — be- (by) plus geond (yonder). Literally by yonder, on the far side.
biblical_def: Beyond does two opposite jobs in Scripture, and both are doctrinally serious. First, it names a boundary that cannot be crossed, and the mouth that says so is a hireling prophet's: “If Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot go beyond the word of the LORD my God, to do less or more” (Num 22:18). Balaam wants the fee and knows the limit, and the whole tragicomedy of Numbers 22-24 is a man testing a boundary that will not move. Second, it names a distance the believer does not have to travel: “Neither is it beyond the sea, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go over the sea for us, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it?” (Deu 30:13) — the commandment is not far off; it is nigh, in the mouth and in the heart, and Paul takes the passage up in Romans 10 and applies it to the word of faith which is preached. Geographically the word simply marks the far side of Jordan (Deu 3:25) or of the Euphrates, where Joshua reminds Israel that “your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time… and they served other gods” (Josh 24:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines beyond as on the further side of, at a distance not yet reached, and also as above or exceeding — past the reach or comprehension of.
webster_full: BEYOND, prep. On the further side of; on the side most distant, at any indefinite distance from that side.
Beyond Jordan.
2. Before; at a place not yet reached.
3. Past; out of reach of; farther than any given limit; as, beyond our power.
4. Above; exceeding to a greater degree; as, this is beyond all praise.
scriptures: And Balaam answered and said unto the servants of Balak, If Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot go beyond the word of the LORD my God, to do less or more.
Neither is it beyond the sea, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go over the sea for us, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it?
Deu 3:25
I pray thee, let me go over, and see the good land that is beyond Jordan, that goodly mountain, and Lebanon.
Josh 24:2

And Joshua said unto all the people, Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods.
corruption_summary: Balaam is treated as a sincere prophet obstructed by circumstance, and Deu 30 is claimed by moralists as proof that the law is easy — against Paul's own use of the passage.
corruption_paragraphs: Balaam says orthodox things and is condemned throughout the rest of Scripture: Peter names “the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness” (2Pe 2:15), Jude names his error, and Revelation names his doctrine, by which he taught Balak to cast a stumblingblock before Israel (Rev 2:14). A man may confess the limits of God's word with perfect accuracy and spend his life probing them for an opening. The lesson is uncomfortable for anyone whose theology is better than his heart: correct doctrine about God's sovereignty is not the same as submission to it.

Deu 30:11-14 has been used by moralists from Pelagius onward to argue that the commandment is within natural human reach, since it is not in heaven nor beyond the sea. Paul's handling in Rom 10:6-8 rules that out. He applies the passage not to the law's attainability but to the nearness of the word of faith which we preach — Christ need not be brought down from above nor up from the dead, because He has already come and already risen, and what remains is confession and belief. The nearness is the gospel's, not the law's.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon begeondan, by yonder; rendering Hebrew eber (H5676), the region across, from abar, to pass over — the root behind Hebrew itself.
roots_lines: Hebrew abar (H5674) — to pass over, cross; the verb behind “go over” and, in one long tradition, behind the name Ibri, Hebrew, the man from across the river.
Hebrew eber (H5676) — the region beyond, the other side; eber hayarden, beyond Jordan.
Num 22:18 — Hebrew lo ukal laabor eth pi YHWH, “I am not able to pass over the mouth of the LORD”; the boundary is His spoken word.
Josh 24:2-3 — “the other side of the flood” is the Euphrates; Abraham is called out from beyond it, from a family that served other gods.
Rom 10:6-8 — Paul's citation of Deu 30:12-14, referred to Christ's incarnation and resurrection rather than to the law's attainability.
usage: “I cannot go beyond the word of the LORD” — true, correct, and said by a man probing for an opening.
“Neither is it beyond the sea” — the word is nigh thee; nobody must fetch it.
“Beyond Jordan” — the good land Moses saw and did not enter.

pos: adv. and prep. (lengthwise; onward beside a line — in Scripture the word for a border traced and a road kept to)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon andlang — and- (against, facing) plus lang (long): literally extending the length of. The sense of accompanying (come along) grew out of the sense of running beside.
biblical_def: Along is a surveyor's word and a traveller's word. In Joshua and Numbers it traces the inheritance line by line: “your south quarter shall be from the wilderness of Zin along by the coast of Edom” (Num 34:3); the border “goeth out from Bethel to Luz, and passeth along unto the borders of Archi to Ataroth” (Josh 16:2). Whole chapters of Scripture consist of such lines, and they exist because the land was not seized but allotted — every tribe received a described portion from the hand of God, and a described portion can be defended against a neighbour's encroachment. In Deuteronomy the word governs a promise of restraint: Israel asks passage of Sihon with the pledge, “I will go along by the high way, I will neither turn unto the right hand nor to the left” (Deu 2:27) — a people with a divine title to Canaan binding themselves not to touch what was not theirs on the road. And in Exodus it describes the seventh plague, where “the fire ran along upon the ground” (Exo 9:23), lightning running level with the hail.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines along as by the length, lengthwise, in a line with the length — and, as a preposition, by the side of, or in the direction of the length of a thing.
webster_full: ALONG, adv. By the length; lengthwise; in a line with the length; as, the fence runs along the road.
2. Onward; in a line, or with a progressive motion; as, come along.
ALONG, prep. By the side of; lengthwise of; as, to walk along the shore.
Note. From the Saxon andlang, extending the whole length of.
scriptures: Num 34:3
Then your south quarter shall be from the wilderness of Zin along by the coast of Edom, and your south border shall be the outmost coast of the salt sea eastward:
Josh 16:2
And goeth out from Bethel to Luz, and passeth along unto the borders of Archi to Ataroth,
Deu 2:27
Let me pass through thy land: I will go along by the high way, I will neither turn unto the right hand nor to the left.
Exo 9:23
And Moses stretched forth his rod toward heaven: and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground; and the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt.
corruption_summary: The boundary chapters are dismissed as tedious land records, when they are the legal charter of a doctrine Scripture takes very seriously: that property is allotted, bounded, and not to be moved.
corruption_paragraphs: Readers skip the border lists, and in skipping them lose the theology of the landmark. Israel's inheritance was assigned by lot — that is, by God (Pro 16:33) — and described so exactly that a man could tell where his neighbour's portion began. That is why moving a landmark is not a minor offence but a cursed one: “Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour's landmark” (Deu 27:17). The boundary chapters are the reason the law of property could be enforced, and the reason Naboth could tell Ahab that the LORD forbid it that he should give the inheritance of his fathers.

Deu 2:27 shows the restraint that follows. Israel is marching to take a land God has given them, and on the way they offer to keep to the highway and touch nothing of Sihon's — because a title to Canaan is not a title to everything. The instinct is precisely what expansionist readings of the conquest deny, and it also rebukes the opposite modern error, which reads the conquest as a template for national aggression. The land was given by name and by border; what lay along the road belonged to somebody else.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon andlang, extending the length of; rendering Hebrew border-verbs such as abar (H5674), to pass over, and taar (H8388), to mark out a boundary.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon andlang — and- facing + lang long; extending the whole length of a thing.
Hebrew abar (H5674) — to pass over or through; used of a border passing along from point to point.
Hebrew taar (H8388) — to mark out, delineate a boundary; the technical verb of the allotment chapters.
Hebrew gebul (H1366) — border, boundary; the noun the border chapters exist to fix.
Hebrew derek hammelek — “the king's high way” (Num 20:17; Deu 2:27), the established road Israel pledged to keep to.
usage: “Along by the coast of Edom” — an inheritance described so it can be defended.
“I will go along by the high way” — a people with a title to Canaan touching nothing of Sihon's.
“The fire ran along upon the ground” — lightning level with the hail in the seventh plague.
